triage.name: Heartburn
triage.reason: Very common symptom presentation with retrosternal burning and regurgitation; students must distinguish GERD from cardiac chest pain.

demographics: Very common in adults; prevalence increases with age
Equally common in men and women overall, though women more often report symptoms
More common in people with obesity

risk_factors.text: Family history of GERD or reflux

family_history: GERD or frequent heartburn in a parent or sibling
social_history: Late-night eating or lying down soon after meals

chief_complaints.text: My chest burns after I eat
I get a sour taste in my throat
It feels like food is coming back up
My stomach feels full and uncomfortable

hpi.onset: Gradual; often after a large meal, lying down, or bending over
hpi.duration: Episodes last minutes to a few hours; recurrent over weeks to months
hpi.progression: Intermittent at first, then more frequent and predictable with meals or position changes; may become daily
hpi.location: Behind the breastbone (retrosternal), sometimes rising into the throat
hpi.radiation: Can radiate upward to the neck, throat, or jaw; does not radiate to the arm or shoulder
hpi.quality: Burning or warm, sometimes described as pressure or tightness
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; usually 3–6/10, worse after big meals
hpi.timing: Within 30–60 minutes after eating; worse when lying down or bending forward; often at night
relieving: Sleeping with the head of the bed elevated

associated_symptoms.text: Sour or bitter taste in the mouth (regurgitation)
Feeling of food or liquid coming back up
Chronic dry cough or throat clearing
Hoarseness or sore throat in the morning

pertinent_negatives: Chest pain with exertion or emotional stress
Chest pain radiating to the left arm or shoulder
Pain that wakes them from sleep and is not relieved by sitting up

positives.text: Feeling full or uncomfortable after meals

argues_against: Weight loss with dysphagia suggests malignancy or stricture

negatives: Chest pain radiating to the arm or jaw
argues_against: Exertional chest pain relieved by rest suggests angina
Chest pain with shortness of breath and diaphoresis suggests acute coronary syndrome
Pleuritic pain with shortness of breath suggests pulmonary embolism or pneumonia

positives.text: Hoarseness or sore throat in the morning

negatives: Lump in the throat that is constant
argues_against: Progressive dysphagia suggests stricture, ring, or cancer

positives.text: Regurgitation of sour or bitter fluid

negatives: Abdominal pain localized to the right upper or lower quadrant
argues_against: Hematemesis or melena suggests ulcer or variceal bleeding
Right upper quadrant pain suggests biliary disease

negatives: Pain worse with deep breath or twisting
argues_against: Reproducible chest wall tenderness suggests costochondritis or musculoskeletal pain
Focal neurologic symptoms suggest a vascular or neurologic cause

atypical.how_it_differs: May present with less burning and more vague chest pressure, cough, or poor appetite; cardiac causes must be excluded first.

Very common in the third trimester due to increased abdominal pressure and hormonal relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter; symptoms often worsen as pregnancy progresses and resolve after delivery.
Infants and young children cannot describe burning; they may present with frequent spitting up, irritability after feeds, arching of the back, poor weight gain, or chronic cough.
Symptoms are often more frequent and severe, with more regurgitation and nighttime symptoms; weight loss improves symptoms.

general.mild: Comfortable, in no distress; able to talk and move freely
general.moderate: Mild discomfort, occasionally placing a hand on the chest or throat; not toxic-appearing
general.severe: Uncomfortable and restless, leaning forward or sitting upright for relief; still not toxic-appearing
general.critical: Ill-appearing and diaphoretic if a cardiac cause is present; otherwise this presentation is not typical of uncomplicated heartburn

findings.finding: Mild epigastric tenderness without guarding or rebound

findings.maneuver: Palpate all four quadrants, checking for guarding, rebound and organomegaly
findings.finding: Soft, non-tender abdomen without guarding, rebound, mass or organomegaly

findings.maneuver: Press under the right costal margin while the patient takes a deep breath (Murphy sign)
findings.finding: No arrest of inspiration and no right upper quadrant tenderness

findings.maneuver: Palpate the sternum, costochondral junctions and anterior chest wall
Auscultate the heart and palpate the peripheral pulses
findings.finding: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmur, rub or gallop, and symmetric pulses
Clear breath sounds without crackles or wheezing

findings.maneuver: Inspect the neck for jugular venous distension at 45 degrees
Press over the dorsum of each foot and the pretibial area
Inspect the oropharynx and posterior pharynx
findings.finding: Mild posterior pharyngeal erythema or a coated tongue, without exudate or swelling

findings.maneuver: Screen cranial nerves, strength and sensation

labs.caveat: Normal. Ordered to exclude acute coronary syndrome when chest pain could be cardiac; a normal troponin with a non-ischemic ECG makes ACS very unlikely.
Anemia suggests chronic reflux esophagitis with occult blood loss or a peptic ulcer rather than uncomplicated heartburn.
Negative. Checked in anyone who could be pregnant before imaging or endoscopy; pregnancy itself is a common cause of heartburn.

findings.finding: No ST elevation or depression; no ischemic changes
Normal PR and QRS intervals without block
ECG is obtained to exclude acute coronary syndrome; a normal tracing supports a non-cardiac cause

imaging.preferred_when: Alarm features (dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, bleeding, anemia) or failure of empiric therapy

findings.text: Mucosal breaks or erosions in the distal esophagus (erosive esophagitis)
Peptic ulcer in the stomach or duodenum
Barrett esophagus (salmon-colored columnar mucosa above the gastroesophageal junction)

imaging.preferred_when: Dysphagia or suspected structural abnormality when endoscopy is not immediately available

findings.text: Reflux of contrast from stomach into esophagus

imaging.preferred_when: Chest pain with concern for a pulmonary or cardiac cause

findings.text: Normal heart size and clear lung fields
Findings suggesting an alternative cause (e.g., pneumonia, pneumothorax, widened mediastinum)

imaging.preferred_when: Symptoms persist despite therapy or diagnosis is uncertain before surgery

findings.text: Increased esophageal acid exposure (abnormal DeMeester score)
Normal acid exposure, suggesting a non-reflux cause

initial.why: Excludes acute coronary syndrome in anyone with chest pain before attributing symptoms to reflux
Cardiac marker to rule out myocardial injury when chest pain could be cardiac
initial.only_if: chest pain could be cardiac or risk factors for coronary disease are present

initial.why: Looks for anemia from occult gastrointestinal blood loss
Rules out pregnancy before imaging or endoscopy and explains symptoms in pregnancy

confirmatory.why: Directly visualizes reflux esophagitis, stricture, ulcer or malignancy
confirmatory.only_if: alarm features (dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, bleeding, anemia) or failure of empiric therapy

confirmatory.why: Confirms pathologic acid reflux when the diagnosis is uncertain or surgery is considered
confirmatory.only_if: symptoms persist despite therapy or diagnosis remains unclear

supporting.why: Evaluates structure and hiatal hernia when dysphagia is present
Screens for a pulmonary cause of chest pain
supporting.only_if: cough, fever or pleuritic features suggest a respiratory cause

not_indicated.why: Not needed unless pain is epigastric and radiates to the back, suggesting pancreatitis
No role in typical meal-related burning chest pain
Not routine for uncomplicated heartburn without respiratory symptoms

decision_points: Exclude acute coronary syndrome first in any patient with chest pain and cardiac risk factors
Pregnancy test before endoscopy or imaging in anyone who could be pregnant
Endoscopy is reserved for alarm features or failure of empiric acid suppression
Trial of lifestyle changes and acid suppression is appropriate when no alarm features are present

differential.name: Acute coronary syndrome
differential.why_considered: Retrosternal chest pain or pressure that can be mistaken for heartburn, especially in older adults or those with cardiac risk factors
differential.trigger: Chest pain that is exertional, associated with shortness of breath, diaphoresis, nausea, or radiation to the arm, shoulder, or jaw

history: Pain brought on by exertion or emotional stress and relieved by rest or nitroglycerin
Pressure, tightness, or heaviness rather than burning
Radiation to the left arm, shoulder, or jaw
Associated shortness of breath, diaphoresis, or nausea
Cardiac risk factors such as hypertension, diabetes, smoking, or family history of early coronary disease
exam: New murmur, S3 gallop, or rales suggesting heart failure
labs: Elevated BNP if heart failure is present
imaging: Regional wall motion abnormality on echocardiography
ecg: New Q waves or conduction abnormalities

differential.name: Peptic ulcer disease
differential.why_considered: Epigastric burning pain that can be confused with reflux, especially if it occurs after meals or at night
differential.trigger: Epigastric pain that is gnawing, occurs between meals or at night, and is relieved by food or antacids

history: Pain localized to the epigastrium rather than retrosternal
Pain relieved by eating (duodenal ulcer) or worsened by eating (gastric ulcer)
Nighttime pain that wakes the patient
History of NSAID use or Helicobacter pylori infection
Melena or hematemesis if bleeding occurs
exam: Signs of anemia such as pallor
labs: Positive H. pylori stool antigen or breath test
Elevated lipase if pancreatitis is present
imaging: Gastric or duodenal ulcer on esophagogastroduodenoscopy
Free air on upright chest x-ray if perforated

differential.name: Biliary colic or cholecystitis
differential.why_considered: Right upper quadrant or epigastric pain that can radiate to the chest or back and be mistaken for reflux

history: Pain in the right upper quadrant or epigastrium, often after fatty meals
Pain radiating to the right shoulder or back
Nausea and vomiting
Fever if cholecystitis is present
exam: Jaundice if common bile duct obstruction is present
labs: Elevated lipase or amylase if pancreatitis is present
imaging: Gallstones or gallbladder wall thickening on ultrasound
Pericholecystic fluid or sonographic Murphy sign

differential.name: Esophageal motility disorder (achalasia or diffuse esophageal spasm)
differential.why_considered: Chest pain and dysphagia that can mimic reflux, especially when symptoms are not clearly meal-related

history: Dysphagia to both solids and liquids
Regurgitation of undigested food
Chest pain that may be provoked by swallowing
Weight loss
exam: Signs of weight loss or malnutrition in advanced cases
imaging: Bird-beak appearance on barium swallow in achalasia
Absent peristalsis and failure of lower esophageal sphincter relaxation on manometry
Corkscrew esophagus in diffuse esophageal spasm

differential.name: Costochondritis
differential.why_considered: Anterior chest pain that can be confused with heartburn, especially if it is sharp or positional

history: Sharp, localized chest pain
Worse with deep breathing, coughing, or twisting
Reproducible by pressing on the chest wall
No relation to meals or lying down
exam: Reproducible tenderness over the costochondral junctions

differential.name: Pneumonia
differential.why_considered: Chest pain and cough that can be mistaken for reflux-related cough or chest discomfort

history: Fever, chills, and productive cough
Pleuritic chest pain worse with deep breath
Shortness of breath
Recent upper respiratory infection
exam: Crackles or bronchial breath sounds on auscultation
imaging: Lobar consolidation or infiltrate on chest x-ray
Consolidation on CT chest if needed

severity.mild: Intermittent symptoms less than twice a week; brief episodes after large meals or lying down; relieved by antacids; no interference with daily activities or sleep
severity.moderate: Symptoms more than twice a week but not daily; episodes last longer and may wake the patient at night; some interference with sleep or daily activities; responds to lifestyle changes and acid suppression
severity.severe: Daily symptoms with frequent nighttime awakenings; significant interference with sleep, work, or eating; may have regurgitation and chronic cough; requires daily acid suppression and evaluation for complications
severity.critical: Not typical of uncomplicated heartburn; if chest pain is crushing, associated with diaphoresis, shortness of breath, or syncope, treat as acute coronary syndrome until proven otherwise

red_flags.finding: Chest pain that is crushing, pressure-like, or associated with diaphoresis, shortness of breath, or syncope
red_flags.meaning: Possible acute coronary syndrome; obtain ECG and troponin immediately
Suggests stricture, ring, or malignancy; needs endoscopy
Suggests malignancy, stricture, or severe esophagitis; needs endoscopy
Suggests gastrointestinal bleeding from esophagitis, ulcer, or varices; needs urgent evaluation
Suggests chronic blood loss from esophagitis or ulcer; needs endoscopy
Suggests obstruction, severe esophagitis, or another cause; needs evaluation

complications.name: Barrett esophagus
clues: Found on endoscopy as salmon-colored mucosa above the gastroesophageal junction

special_populations.differences: May present with less burning and more vague chest pressure, cough, or poor appetite; cardiac causes must be excluded first.

Very common in the third trimester due to increased abdominal pressure and hormonal relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter; symptoms often worsen as pregnancy progresses and resolve after delivery; treat with lifestyle changes and antacids, avoiding certain medications.
Infants and young children cannot describe burning; they may present with frequent spitting up, irritability after feeds, arching of the back, poor weight gain, or chronic cough.
Symptoms are often more frequent and severe, with more regurgitation and nighttime symptoms; weight loss improves symptoms.

key_questions.question: Can you describe the burning sensation and exactly where you feel it?
key_questions.looking_for: Retrosternal burning behind the breastbone, sometimes rising into the throat

key_questions.question: When does it happen in relation to meals, and does lying down or bending over bring it on?
key_questions.looking_for: Within 30–60 minutes after eating; worse lying flat or bending forward; often at night

key_questions.question: What makes it better?
key_questions.looking_for: Antacids, sitting upright, standing, drinking water, elevating the head of the bed

key_questions.question: Do you get a sour or bitter taste in your mouth or feel food coming back up?
key_questions.looking_for: Regurgitation of sour or bitter fluid, water brash

key_questions.question: Is the pain brought on by exertion or emotional stress, and is it relieved by rest?
key_questions.looking_for: Exertional pattern suggests angina rather than reflux

key_questions.question: Does the pain radiate to your arm, shoulder, or jaw, or come with shortness of breath, sweating, or nausea?
key_questions.looking_for: Radiation and associated symptoms suggest acute coronary syndrome

key_questions.question: Any trouble swallowing, painful swallowing, vomiting blood, or black tarry stools?
key_questions.looking_for: Alarm features suggesting stricture, ulcer, or malignancy

key_questions.question: Have you lost weight without trying?
key_questions.looking_for: Unintentional weight loss suggests malignancy or severe esophagitis

key_questions.question: How often do you get this, and does it wake you at night?
key_questions.looking_for: More than twice a week suggests GERD; nighttime awakenings suggest more severe reflux

key_questions.question: What do you eat and drink, and how close to bedtime do you eat?
key_questions.looking_for: Spicy, fatty, or acidic foods, caffeine, chocolate, alcohol, late-evening meals

key_questions.question: Do you smoke or drink alcohol?
key_questions.looking_for: Both are modifiable triggers and risk factors for reflux

key_questions.question: Which medications do you take, including over-the-counter pain relievers?
key_questions.looking_for: NSAIDs, aspirin, prednisone, calcium channel blockers, nitrates, anticholinergics

key_questions.question: Have you had reflux, a hiatal hernia, or an ulcer before?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior GERD, hiatal hernia, or peptic ulcer disease

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have frequent heartburn or GERD?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of GERD or reflux

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy is a common cause of heartburn and affects medication and imaging choices

key_questions.question: Any chronic cough, throat clearing, hoarseness, or sore throat in the morning?

reasoning_points: Retrosternal burning that occurs within an hour of meals and is worse when lying down or bending over
Relief with antacids, sitting upright, or standing
Regurgitation of sour or bitter fluid or a sour taste in the mouth
Absence of exertional chest pain, radiation to the arm or jaw, shortness of breath, or diaphoresis
Absence of alarm features such as dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, hematemesis, or melena
Normal cardiac and abdominal examination without reproducible chest wall tenderness
Normal ECG and troponin when a cardiac cause is a concern
Symptoms recurring more than twice a week suggest GERD rather than occasional heartburn

easy: Classic retrosternal burning after a large meal
Worse lying flat and relieved by antacids
No alarm features and a normal examination
medium: Older adult with chest pressure and cardiac risk factors requiring ECG and troponin first
Nighttime symptoms with chronic dry cough or hoarseness
Symptoms more than twice a week suggesting GERD
Mild epigastric tenderness with a normal cardiac workup
hard: Pregnant patient in the third trimester with new symptoms
Obesity with frequent regurgitation and nighttime symptoms
Patient on NSAIDs or calcium channel blockers with symptoms attributed to medication
Symptoms that persist despite lifestyle changes and acid suppression, requiring endoscopy
Chest pain that is not clearly meal-related and could be cardiac or esophageal in origin
